concepts.title: Soil, Stains and Their Removal
concepts.definition: Fabrics gather two kinds of soil: everyday dust and grease, and accidental stains -- tea, ink, curry, blood, rust. Each stain has a chemistry: fresh stains yield to prompt treatment; protein stains like blood need cold water; grease needs solvents; tannin stains like tea need acids. The rule is act fast and treat by type.
concepts.key_idea: Match the remedy to the stain -- cold for blood, solvent for grease, acid for tea -- and never let a stain set.

solution_steps.explain: Ask what caused it -- grease, protein, tannin, dye or mineral -- since each class needs its own solvent or reagent.
Blot fresh stains, work the remover from the edge inward, and avoid hot water that sets protein stains.
Rinse after treatment and inspect before drying, since heat fixes any residue left behind.

concepts.title: Laundering: Washing, Drying and Ironing by Fabric
concepts.definition: Regular laundering follows a cycle -- sorting, soaking, washing, rinsing, drying, finishing -- tuned to the fabric: cottons bear vigorous washing and hot ironing; silks and woollens demand mild detergent, gentle handling and low heat. Sorting by colour and fabric protects the whole wash.
concepts.key_idea: Sort, soak, wash, rinse, dry, press -- with the vigour scaled down for silk and wool, up for cotton.

solution_steps.explain: Separate whites from colours, cottons from delicates; mend and empty pockets before soaking.
Use the mildest effective method -- gentle kneading for silk and wool, rubbing and machine action only for sturdy cottons.
Shape woollens flat away from sun, line-dry colours in shade, and iron each fabric at its safe temperature.

concepts.title: Storage and Long-Term Care of Fabrics
concepts.definition: Between uses, fabrics need storage that blocks their enemies -- moisture, insects, dust and sunlight. Clean items only are stored; woollens get washed, sunned and packed with repellents; silks are wrapped; and periodic airing keeps long-stored textiles fresh and safe.
concepts.key_idea: Clean before you store, keep out damp, light and moths -- and visit the trunk between seasons.

solution_steps.explain: Launder or dry-clean before storage -- soil and stains feed insects and set permanently over time.
Pack dry items in breathable covers with repellents, away from damp walls and direct light.
Open trunks on dry, sunny days to refresh fabrics and spot trouble early.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student spills ink on a white cotton shirt. Give the removal steps in order.

solution_template.explain: Blot the excess at once -- never rub, which spreads the dye deeper.
Treat with a suitable stain remover or mild acid solution, working from the stain's edge inward.
Rinse thoroughly and inspect before any drying, repeating if a shadow remains.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A family packs woollen sweaters away for summer. List the correct storage steps and the mistakes to avoid.

solution_template.explain: Unwashed wool invites moths; trapped damp invites mildew -- so clean and sun-dry first.
Fold with repellent sachets in breathable bags, stored in a cool dry shelf.
Air the packed woollens on dry days and renew repellents mid-season.
